identityReview: Samantha Power, born 1970; current Harvard HLS/HKS practice professor, former US ambassador to the United Nations and former USAID administrator. Officially confirmed birth year and migration from Ireland are retained; conflicting precise birthplaces and birthday are not resolved. Yale BA and Harvard JD are earned degrees, distinct from research doctorates. UN ambassador represents the United States rather than being a UN Secretariat employee.
lifeStatusEvidence: AP’s September 2026 report describes her actual CGI address on childhood lead-poisoning prevention partnerships. Search metadata supplies 25 September publication, while the body says Wednesday; the biography only asserts September activity, not an exact day inferred from unrelated photo captions. The current Harvard faculty entry corroborates her role.

sourceReview.accessMethod: Read current HLS faculty biography, Carnegie Council biography, Pulitzer winner entry, Obama archive, Senate confirmation record, State Historian mission record, historical MCC appointment biography, selected original Senate hearing passages, HLS appointment retrospective and May announcement, and AP current reporting. Read Commons image description, public-domain notice and upload history; original image/source were inaccessible.
corrections: Read current HLS faculty profile: William D. Zabel human-rights practice professorship and joint Anna Lindh HKS appointment; Yale BA 1992, Harvard JD 1999; immigration from Ireland at nine. USAID service 2021–2025, UN 2013–2017 and NSC 2009–2013 are historical. JD is a professional law degree, not research PhD. Current bibliography confirms the 2002 genocide book and 2019 memoir. Institutional claims about vaccine quantities, hunger prevention and Ukraine outcomes are not independently audited or credited solely to Power. Scheduled 2027 teaching is not treated as already delivered.

Read Carnegie Council biography: reporting on former Yugoslav wars from 1993 to 1996 and founding executive directorship of Carr Center, listed as 1998–2002. Harvard’s 2017 announcement separately describes a 1998 initiative that became the center; other center pages use 1999 founding. The profile avoids equating preparatory appointment and institutional founding. Carnegie’s separate book-critics-award claim is not used without the award body’s record.

Read official Pulitzer winner page: 2003 General Nonfiction for A Problem from Hell. The 2002 publication date is separately supplied by HLS. Old biographical language on the prize page is not a current job record. Read the winner listing and book description, not the full book; no long extracts or automatic inference of later policy effectiveness.

Read archived Obama White House biography describing her then-current UN ambassadorship and prior special-assistant/senior-director role for multilateral affairs and human rights. It is an archived administration record, not evidence of officeholding in 2026 or employment by the UN Secretariat. The current HLS profile provides the NSC date range.

Read Senate roll-call 200, 1 August 2013, 14:38: confirmation approved 87 yeas, 10 nays, three not voting. This is Senate confirmation, distinct from formal appointment and credentials. No claim that 87–10 was a UN election or a popular mandate.

Read State Department Historian record: birth year 1970; appointed 2 August 2013, credentials 5 August 2013, mission termination 21 January 2017. Database notice says updates suspended, so used for this historical mission, not current leadership. Conflicting secondary birthplace claims (London, Dublin, Castleknock and Dungarvan) are not resolved by popularity; precise date and place are omitted, while Harvard supports immigration from Ireland.

Read MCC’s historical biography: sworn in 3 May 2021 as 19th USAID administrator. Its present/future-tense descriptions belong to the original appointment context, not current 2026 tenure. HLS confirms service ended in 2025. No statement that aid appropriations, implementing partners’ work or institutional outcomes were personal achievements alone.

Read hearing front matter and selected Gaza exchanges in the original Senate Foreign Relations FY2025 USAID budget hearing of 10 April 2024, notably printed pages 26–27. Power agrees with Kaine’s concern about famine risk and discusses child malnutrition and urgent access. This is the Senate hearing, not the separate House exchange with Castro that same day. Senator statements and appended journalism are not silently attributed to Power. Not a full hearing/appendix audit or independent reclassification of famine; no legal finding is inferred. A later direct download request exceeded the tool’s PDF size limit, but indexed original text was available and read.

Read HLS’s 17 July 2025 retrospective confirming return on 1 June and joint HLS/HKS roles, with previous joint service 2017–2021. Also read the 16 May 2025 prospective announcement. Announcement, effective return and July retrospective are distinct; the current faculty page independently confirms ongoing employment.

Read AP’s actual September 2026 CGI reporting: Power spoke about continuing childhood lead-poisoning prevention partnerships after US aid cuts. Search metadata dates the report 25 September; the body says Wednesday. The profile uses month precision rather than inferring an exact speech day from another attendee’s photograph. Official CGI Flickr search metadata corroborates a 23 September closing session but direct opening failed and no event photograph/video was inspected. Neither funding pledges nor the speech prove all aid losses were replaced or lead exposure eliminated.
